articles.title: FCC boss signals major crackdown on TV networks pushing 'fake polls' ahead of the midterms
articles.summary: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr says the agency may soon issue guidance to broadcast TV networks over airing what he called "fake polls" before midterms.
articles.body: The Federal Communications Commission could soon issue guidance to broadcast television networks over what FCC Chairman Brendan Carr called "fake polls" ahead of the midterms. Speaking on "The Sunday Briefing," Carr argued that broadcast television is subject to different federal requirements than cable channels or online platforms because stations operate under FCC licenses. "The one thing that President Trump gets, fundamentally, is that broadcast TV is completely different than other forms of distribution, including cable," Carr said Sunday. FCC CHAIR SUGGESTS ABC SKIPPING TRUMP'S SPEECH WILL FACTOR IN LICENSE RENEWAL DECISION "And so many broadcasters right now, they [want to] break the deal that they cut with the American people. They get billions of dollars in taxpayer, effectively, subsidized distribution. And what they're supposed to do in exchange is operate in the public interest, not some sort of narrow partisan interest," he added. His comments come after President Donald Trump criticized NBC News’s Kristen Welker on August 30 over what he said was a mischaracterization of his endorsement record in political primaries. Welker, speaking during a segment on a local NBC affiliate, noted that Trump would "loom large" over the midterms before pointing to his endorsement record. DEMS DERIDED TRUMP’S MIDTERM GAMBLE — UNTIL HE ENDED UP WINNING BIG "He, of course, has endorsed a slate of candidates in the primaries," Welker said. "He's had some mixed results, but most recently, his pick of Senator Darline Graham, of course, the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, was successful in her primary battle." Trump responded on Truth Social, writing, "Kristen Welker, the Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press, just stated that Donald Trump has ‘mixed results’ on his Endorsements of Candidates," before pointing to his endorsement record, including his backing of Sen. Darline Graham. NEW YORK TIMES BLASTS ‘ABUSIVE’ TRUMP SUBPOENAS TARGETING REPORTERS’ SOURCES "How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment," he added. NBC News defended Welker in a statement to Fox News Digital, backing its "Meet the Press" moderator following Trump’s threat. "Kristen is one of the best in the business, and we stand by her," an NBC News spokesperson said. MYSTERIOUS POLLING FIRM BEHIND FAKE ELECTION SURVEYS CLOSES AFTER ADMITTING ‘SOCIAL EXPERIMENT’ Carr said there has been particular interest in reminding broadcasters about their obligations regarding what he called "fake polls," which he warned could be used to suppress voters heading into the fall midterms. "I think President Trump is over the target, and we're looking at a lot of actions. For instance, there's a lot of interest right now in fake polls that are out there," Carr said. "And so the FCC may put guidance out soon to remind broadcasters about their obligations with respect to not airing fake polls, particularly if they're done to suppress people heading into the fall," he added.DON'T LET FAKE ELECTION WEBSITES FOOL YOU BEFORE 2026 MIDTERMS FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez publicly rejected the idea of penalizing reporters, posting on X: "As I've said many times, the FCC has no authority to punish journalists this administration doesn’t like. These threats to press freedom are dangerous. They undermine the foundation of our democracy, and they have no place in it." articles.title: Mooney M20F small plane crashes near Florida airport; pilot killed
articles.summary: US News: A Mooney M20F small plane tragically crashed near Space Coast Regional Airport in Titusville, Florida, resulting in the death of the pilot. The NTSB is investigating the incident which occurred on Monday morning. Authorities closed nearby roads and cut electricity as a precaution. This incident follows another aviation disaster at Miami International Airport.
articles.body: A pilot was killed after a small aircraft crashed near Space Coast Regional Airport in Titusville, Florida, on Monday morning, Florida Today reported.The plane was identified by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) as a Mooney M20F, a four-seat propeller aircraft. The agency is investigating the crash.The aircraft came down on a road near the airport at around 10 a.m. local time, according to police. Footage from the scene showed the plane engulfed in flames, while authorities closed the road in both directions.The Titusville Police Department said electricity was cut to nearby areas as a precaution by Florida Power and Light following the crash.Titusville is about 40 miles east of Orlando on Florida’s Atlantic coast.The circumstances that led to the crash were not immediately known. Investigators from the NTSB are expected to examine the wreckage as part of the investigation.The crash occurred less than 24 hours after an Amazon cargo aircraft overshot the runway at Miami International Airport. Five people were killed and five others seriously injured after the Boeing 767-300 crossed a road beyond the runway and struck several vehicles.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: An Australian woman learned she was pregnant and could give birth ‘any day’ within 24 hours; her daughter arrived at 21 weeks 3 days and became the country’s most premature baby to survive
articles.summary: Rest of World News: An Australian mother discovered she was pregnant just five days before going into labour, and gave birth less than 24 hours after doctors told her tha.
articles.body: An Australian mother discovered she was pregnant just five days before going into labour, and gave birth less than 24 hours after doctors told her that her baby could arrive at any moment. Her daughter, Makerita Tanuvasa, known by her middle name Miracle, was born at just 21 weeks and three days of pregnancy. Weighing 351 grams, less than a standard tin of soup, and measuring 30.5 centimetres long, she has officially become the most premature baby ever to survive in Australia. The remarkable story, reported by People magazine and regional news outlet 9News, began when Annrose Tanuvasa completed an intense gym challenge but noticed she had lost much less weight than expected. She did not know she was pregnant because she had suffered a miscarriage in December, so she went for a routine ultrasound."The sonographer told us that we were about 22 weeks pregnant. But I told her, I said that's impossible. And she was like, 'Why do you think it's impossible?' And I said, 'Because I had a miscarriage in December'," Tanuvasa recalled during an interview with 9News. "She said, 'Well maybe you had a twin and you miscarried the twin'." Further medical checks showed that Tanuvasa was already in active labour, and doctors estimated that the pregnancy was even earlier than first thought. Within 24 hours, the Queensland mother had to deal with the shock of discovering her unexpected pregnancy and the immediate risk of an extremely premature birth.Fight for survival in neonatal careMiracle was born at a stage when doctors rarely attempt intensive medical treatment or resuscitation because survival chances are extremely low. Her arrival therefore created a major medical challenge. When Tanuvasa first saw her daughter, the baby's tiny size left her overwhelmed. “I took one look at her and I was like, 'There's no way she's going to make it',” Annrose Tanuvasa admitted. "It was just like she was here to fight." Her husband, Misi Tanuvasa, also remembered the shock of seeing their daughter. "We weren't able to hold her, but she was very, very small," he said. Miracle was immediately taken to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital. She was placed inside an incubator and connected to breathing tubes, life-support monitors and delicate medical lines. During the first month, every update from doctors was uncertain. "Every visit, it was like real quiet, like almost like no one wanted to tell us, 'we don't know if she's going to survive or not'," Tanuvasa said. "But I think after one month, it just started to get real bright in the room." Doctors and nurses were amazed by the baby's strength. "Even the doctors couldn't explain how she was able to survive everything she's gone through," Misi said. Tanuvasa recalled one doctor speaking directly to the family about their daughter's unexpected progress: “We can't give you any answers. Everything is actually just a miracle.” That comment inspired the couple to make "Miracle" their daughter's middle name. "And I just said, 'well, let's keep it like that'," Tanuvasa said.Four weeks before the first touchDoctors had to keep physical contact to a minimum because Miracle's skin and organs were extremely underdeveloped. It was four weeks before her parents were allowed to hold her through skin-to-skin contact, also known as kangaroo care. “It was magical, but it was also very scary, holding such a tiny baby,” Tanuvasa said about the emotional moment. Miracle spent 14 weeks in intensive care at Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital before becoming stable enough to move to the special care nursery at Logan Hospital. Medical staff were also struck by how unusual her case was. Registered nurse Renee Judd, who has worked in neonatal nursing for 16 years, said she had never cared for a baby born this early. “I haven't seen a 21-plus-three-weeker,” Judd told 9News. “We've had other little babies here, but not that young, and I have been 16 years in the neonatal journey in Logan.”Leaving hospital after four monthsAfter more than four months in hospital, Miracle was finally well enough to go home with her family. To celebrate the historic moment, doctors, nurses, cleaners and allied health workers lined the hospital corridors and cheered as her parents carried her out. Tanuvasa expressed her gratitude to the medical team that had cared for her daughter throughout the four-month stay. “Thank you guys so much for all the love and care you gave our daughter, the nurses, the doctors, the cleaners, social workers,” Tanuvasa said. “Thank you guys so much for everything.” A typical human pregnancy lasts about 35 to 40 weeks, but advances in specialised neonatal care continue to push the limits of how early a baby can survive. Globally, the youngest known surviving premature baby is Curtis Means, who was born in Alabama, US, in 2020 at 21 weeks and one day, weighing 420 grams. Miracle's survival at 21 weeks and three days has set a new Australian record, surpassing previous national milestones and showing how specialised medical care can produce remarkable outcomes even in extremely difficult circumstances.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Police seek to identify protesters behind Portsmouth anti-migrant disorder
articles.summary: Sarah Jones told MPs the violence sparked by the arrival of 120 migrants in a single dinghy was "intimidating and thuggish".
articles.body:
Police are seeking to identify protesters after several officers were injured and vehicles damaged in Portsmouth at a demonstration sparked by the arrival of 120 migrants in a single dinghy.

Policing Minister Sarah Jones told the House of Commons the disorder on Sunday night was "intimidating and thuggish" and warned "those who cross into illegality" would "face the full force of the law".

The protests followed a large group of masked men holding a demonstration over small-boat crossings at the Port of Dover on Saturday, causing major disruption.

Portsmouth City Council said the Home Office had "serious questions to answer" over the decision to bring the migrants, who had crossed the English Channel from France, to shore in the area.

What we know about anti-migrant protests and organiser Danny Thomas

Watch: Anti-migrant protesters block roads in Portsmouth

Council leader Steve Pitt said the decision had caused "needless disruption".

Around 200 people, some wearing masks, confronted police in riot gear after they descended on the Eastney Landing ferry port area, where the migrants were landed.

Police protected a number of coaches parked on a road leading away from Eastney Marina as protesters blocked traffic. A dispersal order was put in place, meaning anyone failing to comply with police could be arrested.

In a statement, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said a handful of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, none of which were serious.

It said: "Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest.

"No arrests have been made at this time, however an investigation to identify offenders responsible for any assaults to officers, criminal damage to vehicles or other criminal offences has been launched."

Spencer Wragg, chair of Hampshire Police Federation, said: "I've seen footage of officers being pushed off their motorbikes, I've seen pictures of police vehicles damaged. It appears that the police last night became the target for some of the protest."

Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo - an associate of far-right activist Tommy Robinson - was livestreaming from the scene - where he called for his supporters to "get down to Eastney" and stop the migrants being transported.

The coaches carrying the migrants were able to leave in the early hours of Monday and the Border Force confirmed "individuals from the boat have been transported outside of Hampshire for processing".

Footage shared online appeared to show protesters following the convoy of coaches along a motorway after it had left.

Protesters said they were trying to stop authorities transporting the migrants to the Manston processing centre in Kent.

In a statement to the House of Commons on Monday, the policing minister said: "Peaceful protest is a fundamental part of our democracy and it must be defended But so too is the right of other citizens to go about their lives without undue interference – and there can be no excuse for threatening behavior or serious disruption.

Sarah Jones added: "Let me therefore make clear to the House and to the country that disorder of any kind will never be tolerated and those who cross the line from peaceful protest into illegality will face the full force of the law."

Responding, shadow home secretary Chris Philp condemned the violence in Portsmouth but added: "This should also be a wake-up call for the government because it's not just those protesters in Dover and Portsmouth who feel so angry about large-scale illegal immigration.

"It is millions and millions of people up and down this country who feel angry as well."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the country is on the edge of "serious civil disturbance" and called on protests to remain peaceful.

In a video posted to social media, he said: "Peaceful protest: good. Uniforms and masks: bad. Voting is the only way we get a solution."

Some 625 migrants on eight boats were brought to shore at Dover and Portsmouth On Sunday, according to Home Office figures.

A total of 16,513 people arrived in the UK in small boats in the year to 1 September - which is 43% lower than the same period the previous year.

UK net migration has meanwhile dropped to its lowest level outside of the Covid pandemic since 2012.

This weekend's disruption comes just days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.

But while the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies".

In August, a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel.

It is thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area.

articles.title: Russia shutters German consulate as diplomatic freeze deepens
articles.summary: Moscow retaliates after similar move from Berlin last week citing failed drone attack on airport.
articles.body:
Moscow has ordered the closure of the German consulate in St Petersburg.

Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced on Monday that the consulate in the second city must cease operations by September 18.

The order represents a tit-for-tat move, and brings into the open the growing ill feeling between the two countries amid Russia’s war on Ukraine.

Berlin shuttered two Russian diplomatic operations in Germany last week, having accused Moscow of being behind an attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport .

In a statement published on Telegram on Monday, Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Germany has “provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations”, and bears “full responsibility for the consequences”.

Russia has now ordered that all diplomats and staff from the St Petersburg consulate must leave the country by September 18.

On Sunday, Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergey Lavrov denounced Germany for its accusation regarding the drone attack, and asserted that the allegations marked “the beginning of a real war”.

The closure of the German consulate marks a new low in Moscow and Berlin’s diplomatic relations, which have seriously deteriorated since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Germany has emerged as one of Ukraine’s strongest supporters in Europe, allocating more than $50bn in civilian aid for Kyiv and almost $67bn in military assistance, according to its Foreign Ministry.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly condemned the West’s support for Ukraine.

Tensions between Berlin and Moscow increased last week as Germany made the accusation regarding the failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Putin has dismissed the allegations, claiming, without offering details, that the evidence was “planted”.

As it revealed the accusations, Germany ordered the closure of Russia’s consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin.

Moscow retaliated by ordering all branches of Germany’s Goethe-Institut closed. Its staff members have been ordered to leave Russia by Sunday.

Lavrov said Berlin’s closure of Russia’s diplomatic institutions last week reminded him of events that preceded World War II, describing the measures as “absolutely unacceptable” and accusing Germany of wanting “war again”.
